data.content_ref: inline:{"analogy":null,"claim":"The preference smuggles induction back into Popper's system because any claim that a 'better-corroborated' theory is preferable for future action implicitly assumes that past performance predicts future success, which is the very definition of induction Popper sought to eliminate.","counterconditions":[{"case":"If Popper can demonstrate a purely deductive link between surviving a test and being a better candidate for future tests without invoking temporal uniformity.","checker_spec":null,"eval":"observation"},{"case":"If the preference is redefined as purely arbitrary or aesthetic, devoid of predictive expectation.","checker_spec":null,"eval":"observation"},{"case":"If the concept of 'severity' can be defined entirely independently of any inductive background assumptions.","checker_spec":null,"eval":"observation"}],"definitions":[],"derivation":[],"formalization_refs":[],"mechanism":"To prefer Theory A over Theory B because A survived tests that B failed (or A survived more severe tests) is to act on the expectation that A will continue to succeed where B might fail. This expectation is an inductive inference. Without the assumption that the future will resemble the past (uniformity of nature), the fact that A survived yesterday offers no logical reason to expect it to survive tomorrow. Thus, the 'pragmatic' preference is indistinguishable from inductive probabilistic reasoning in practice.","premises":[],"schema":"deepreason-reasoning-envelope-v1","scope":{"covers":[],"excludes":[]},"simulation_refs":[],"uncertainties":[]}
